questions.title: The value of urban trees
questions.prompt: Urban trees do more than improve the appearance of a city. They provide shade, reduce surface temperatures, and create habitats for wildlife. However, successful planting requires careful planning. Local authorities must choose species that can tolerate changing conditions while ensuring that roots have enough space to grow.
questions.explanation: Mark thought groups. Read every word and let punctuation guide your pauses.

questions.title: Why sleep supports learning
questions.prompt: Today we are examining the relationship between sleep and learning. Learning does not end when a student closes a book. During sleep, the brain strengthens some of the connections formed during the day. This process helps new information become more stable and easier to retrieve. Experiments comparing rested students with sleep deprived students often find differences in attention as well as memory. That matters because attention determines how well information is learned in the first place. Studying through the night can therefore be counterproductive. A better approach is to distribute study across several days and maintain a regular sleep schedule. Sleep is not a substitute for study, but it helps the brain use that study effectively.
points: Sleep strengthens connections and consolidates memory
Sleep deprivation reduces attention and memory
Distributed study and regular sleep are more effective than studying all night
questions.model: The lecturer explains that sleep supports learning by strengthening new brain connections and consolidating memories. Lack of sleep also reduces attention, making it harder to learn information initially. The recommended approach is to spread study over several days and keep a regular sleep schedule instead of studying all night.
questions.explanation: Note the main idea and two supporting details. Explain how they connect.

questions.title: Should lectures be recorded?
questions.prompt: Speaker one: I think every lecture should be recorded. When I review a complicated topic, being able to pause and replay the explanation makes a real difference. Last semester I missed two classes because I was ill, and recordings helped me catch up without relying completely on someone else's notes. They also help students who are still becoming familiar with academic English. I do not see recordings as a replacement for attending, but as a second opportunity to understand the material. Speaker two: I can see those benefits, but I am worried about participation. If students know that a recording will be available, some may decide not to attend. That could make discussions less lively. There is also a privacy issue when classmates ask personal questions or share experiences. People may be less willing to contribute if their comments are stored online. I would prefer recordings of the main explanation rather than the entire class. Speaker three: Perhaps we could separate the lecture from the discussion. The lecturer could record the core explanation, then switch off the recording for questions and group activities. Students would still have a reason to attend because the interactive part would only happen in class. Access could be limited to students enrolled in the course, and recordings could be removed at the end of the semester. Speaker one: That sounds reasonable. My main concern is having a reliable explanation to revisit. I would still attend to ask questions and work with other students. It might also help if the lecturer added a short summary of the key ideas alongside each recording. Speaker two: I would support that approach, provided everyone knows when recording is happening. Clear rules about access and deletion would address some of my concerns. We should also check whether attendance changes after the policy is introduced. Speaker three: Then perhaps we agree on a trial. Record the teaching portion, protect discussion time, and ask students and lecturers for feedback after a few weeks. That would let the university evaluate the benefits without committing immediately to recording everything.
points: Speaker one supports recordings for revision and missed classes
Speaker two worries about attendance participation and privacy
Speaker three proposes recording explanations but not discussions
They agree on restricted access and a trial with feedback
questions.model: The students discuss whether lectures should be recorded. The first speaker supports recordings because they help with revision, missed classes, and understanding difficult material. The second raises concerns about attendance and privacy, particularly when students share personal experiences. The third proposes a compromise: record the core explanation but keep discussions private. The others accept this approach, with restricted access and clear rules. They ultimately support a trial followed by feedback and an attendance review.
questions.explanation: Track each speaker's view. Explain agreement, disagreement, and the shared conclusion.

questions.title: Request a deadline extension
questions.prompt: You have a presentation due on Friday, but the data you need will not arrive until Thursday evening. Speak to your lecturer, explain the problem, and request a short extension while showing how you will complete the work.
points: Address the lecturer politely
Explain that the data arrives Thursday evening before a Friday deadline
Request a short extension
Offer a concrete plan to complete the presentation
questions.model: Hello Professor, could I discuss the deadline for Friday's presentation? The data I need will only arrive on Thursday evening, so I am concerned about completing the analysis accurately. Would it be possible to submit on Monday instead? I have already prepared the structure and background, and I can finish the analysis over the weekend. Thank you for considering my request.
questions.explanation: Speak directly to the person. Explain the issue, make your request, and use an appropriate tone.

questions.title: Repair instead of replace
questions.prompt: Many cities are establishing repair cafés where volunteers help residents fix broken household items. The aim is not simply to reduce the cost of replacing appliances. Repairing products also keeps useful materials out of landfill and allows people to share practical knowledge. However, volunteers sometimes struggle to obtain spare parts or technical instructions. Some campaigners therefore argue that manufacturers should be required to make this information available. Such policies could extend product life, but repair services still depend on skilled people and sufficient demand.
points: Repair cafes reduce waste and replacement costs
Volunteers share practical skills
Access to spare parts and instructions is a barrier
Supportive policy and skilled people are needed
questions.explanation: Write one complete sentence in 5–75 words. Preserve the main idea and its relationship to supporting details.

questions.title: From observation to experiment
questions.prompt: Put the paragraphs in the most logical order.
paragraphs: The team first noticed that plants near the window grew faster.
They wondered whether the amount of light explained the difference.
To test this idea, they grew identical plants under different lighting conditions.
The results showed that additional light increased growth within a certain range.
questions.explanation: Observation leads to a hypothesis, then an experiment, then results.

questions.title: The limits of planting
questions.prompt: Coastal wetlands protect communities by absorbing some of the energy of incoming waves. They also provide habitats for fish and birds and store carbon in waterlogged soils. Despite these benefits, many wetlands have been drained or built over. Restoration projects can help, but success depends on understanding local water flows. Simply planting vegetation is unlikely to work if the conditions that support it have disappeared. Long term monitoring is also essential because changes in sea level and nearby development can affect a restored site.
questions.stem: Why might planting vegetation alone fail?
options: Wetlands do not need vegetation.
The supporting water conditions may no longer exist.
Vegetation cannot store carbon.
Monitoring prevents plants from growing.
questions.explanation: Successful restoration depends on the water conditions that support wetland plants.
